The player sits with the instrument on the lap and plucks the strings to accompany a whispered singing voice. In the past it was mostly played by professional musicians for chiefs, with epic and historical songs; in Burundi it was also played at night for the monarch, and it was played to cattle because of a traditional belief that cattle love its sound. The songs concern folk tales, historical events, personal experience and everyday happenings.

Its range runs from the low middle register to the upper middle register, and its notes are clear and well defined. The instrument amplifies the vibration of the strings through the resonance of its trough body, producing a warm sound with a strong local character. Compared with the bright, clean classical guitar, the inanga sounds fuller and more inward; compared with the harp it is gentler and lacks the harp's brilliance, but it has more of an original, plain character. Its overtones are rich and its sound decays naturally, which suits lyrical and quiet melodies and creates a strong African and local atmosphere.

The inanga is a traditional string instrument of East Africa, Hornbostel–Sachs number 322.11, found in Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda and parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It is about 75 cm to 1 m long and 25 to 30 cm wide, with a slightly concave soundboard and a thick notched rim that holds six to eight strings; the strings are mostly natural fibre, now also nylon or metal, and in practice one long string often runs through the notches and is tied to wooden pegs. The player sits with the instrument on the legs and plucks along its whole length, changing the timbre with the plucking position, and almost always sings a repeated melody in a whispered voice. In the past it was mostly played by professional musicians for chiefs, with epic and historical songs; in Burundi it was played at night while the mwami rested, and it was played to cattle too.
伊南加筒琴為東非傳統樂器，見於蒲隆地、盧安達、烏干達及剛果民主共和國部分地區。過: The inanga is a traditional instrument of East Africa, found in Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda and parts of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. It was mostly played by professional musicians for chiefs, mainly in epic and historical songs praising their patron. In Burundi it was traditionally played while the mwami rested at night, and it is considered the earliest instrument invented in that country; in Rwanda it is an important and respected instrument. Playing is mostly a male activity, and children usually learn on their own without formal teaching.
伊南加筒琴的琴身以igiháhe、umwūngo、umukoni或umunyár: The body of the inanga is made from trees such as igiháhe, umwūngo, umukoni or umunyáre, with a slightly concave soundboard and a thick notched rim that holds the strings. The sound source is the strings, made of natural fibre; animal gut or muscle was also used traditionally, and nylon and metal are used today. In practice one long string runs through the notches of the rim and is tied to wooden tuning pegs. The sources do not record the thickness of the soundboard, the other fittings of the rim, or the material of the tuning parts.
演奏者採坐姿，將琴身置於膝上，以手指撥動整條弦發聲；也可在弦的不同位置撥奏，改變: The player sits with the instrument on the lap and sets the whole length of a string sounding with a finger; plucking at different points along the string changes the timbre. Pitch is adjusted by tightening or loosening the string, and the instrument is laid out in a five-note scale. Players usually sing while they play, in short repeated melodic phrases, in a whispered voice. Learning is mostly informal: a father often leaves the instrument in sight and the child works it out alone.
